strengths: Well-motivated and practically important problem: reconstructing language-embedded 3D Gaussians in a single feed-forward pass from uncalibrated, unposed multi-view inputs spanning sparse (2) to dense (32+) views addresses clear limitations of prior feed-forward semantic methods that are restricted to two views or require camera parameters.

The 3D-annotation-free training framework with coverage-based novel-view selection and photometric supervision under a distillation regime is a sensible and non-trivial design that enables training on 2D data at scale.

InstanceMV-14K (15M+ images, ~14K scenes with instance masks) is a valuable resource contribution, and the instance-guided contrastive learning is a clean complexity-reduction trick (O(NpK) vs O(Np^2)) with clear motivation.

The geometry–semantic hierarchical sparsification with moment-matched isotropic semantic Gaussians is a thoughtful technical component that decouples semantic from geometric density; ablations show it cuts semantic Gaussian count (6.4M → 2.6M) without accuracy loss.

Strong quantitative results: consistent improvements over feed-forward baselines across all view counts, and comparison to per-scene optimized methods (LangSplat, LangScene-X) with orders-of-magnitude speedup (seconds vs. 10–20 minutes) while achieving higher query accuracy.
weaknesses: The '3D-annotation-free' framing is somewhat misleading: the framework relies heavily on VGGT pseudo-labels for geometry/camera supervision, so it is better described as pseudo-label distillation. The dependence on VGGT quality (and failure modes when VGGT is wrong on the training distribution) is not analyzed.

Potential train/test leakage is not addressed: InstanceMV-14K is built from ScanNet and ScanNet++, and evaluation is conducted on ScanNet (main results) and ScanNet++ (ablations). The paper does not state whether evaluation scenes overlap with training scenes; this is a critical omission that could inflate reported numbers.

Baseline fairness is questionable: LSM and Uni3R were designed for fixed sparse-view settings and are adapted to dense views via DUSt3R post-processing; their severe degradation at 16/32 views (e.g., Uni3R PSNR dropping to 10.55) may reflect adaptation artifacts rather than method inferiority. A more direct comparison with multi-view-native baselines (e.g., AnySplat-style approaches extended with semantics) would strengthen the case.
3D editing is showcased in Figure 1 as a key capability but receives no experiments, evaluation protocol, or qualitative examples in the paper; this overclaims relative to the evidence.

Ablations are thin: no ablation for the coverage threshold τ, voxel sizes ε_geo/ε_sem, semantic feature dimension D, instance sampling strategy, or the 3D feature aggregation module; only two ablation tables are provided, and they are run on ScanNet++ which may be in the training data.
Evaluation is confined to indoor ScanNet/ScanNet++ scenes, leaving the claimed generalization from Internet-video training data (RealEstate10K) and out-of-distribution scenes empirically unverified.

Missing implementation details hamper reproducibility: semantic feature dimension D, SH degree k, how features are rendered, memory footprint at inference, and the actual sparse/dense-view scaling of runtime and GPU memory are not reported. The project page link is empty.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion is provided despite claims of downstream robotic/AR applicability.

Writing quality issues: several typos ('preatrained', 'are struggle to handle'), inconsistent notation in Eq. (11)–(12), and the LSeg baseline comparison (which consumes ground-truth novel views) conflates 2D segmentation quality with 3D semantic embedding quality.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: feed-forward reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussians supporting both sparse (2) and dense (32+) uncalibrated, unposed views in a single model, which existing feed-forward semantic methods (2-view-only or view-specific) do not handle.

The 3D-annotation-free training recipe is sensible: using VGGT-derived pseudo-labels for geometry plus coverage-based novel-view selection for photometric supervision is a reasonable way to exploit 2D-only data at scale.
InstanceMV-14K (15M images, ~14K scenes with instance masks from scans and Internet video) is a potentially useful resource for the community, enabled by the annotation-free framework.

Reported quantitative results are strong: consistent improvements over feed-forward baselines across view counts (Table 1), and orders-of-magnitude faster reconstruction than per-scene optimization methods (Table 2, seconds vs. tens of minutes) with better mIoU/mAcc.

The geometry-semantic hierarchical sparsification (moment-matched isotropic semantic Gaussians at coarser voxelization) is a reasonable engineering contribution, and ablations indicate it reduces semantic Gaussian count (6.4M → 2.6M) with slight mIoU gain.
weaknesses: Serious evaluation-protocol concern: InstanceMV-14K is built from ScanNet, ScanNet++, ArkitScenes, and RealEstate10K, and the method is evaluated on ScanNet (Table 1) and ScanNet++ (ablations, Table 3). The paper never specifies scene-level train/test splits, so training/test overlap appears likely and would invalidate the headline comparisons. This must be clarified and is potentially disqualifying as written.

Limited novelty relative to prior art: the architecture, initialization, camera/depth heads, and geometric supervision are all inherited from VGGT; the semantic Gaussian head, instance contrastive loss, and hierarchical sparsification are incremental extensions of existing ideas (DPT heads, voxel sparsification à la Scaffold-GS, standard InfoNCE). The core system-level claim is competent but the methodological contribution is thin.

Geometric distillation from VGGT caps achievable geometry quality, yet no geometry metrics (depth/pose accuracy, Chamfer) are reported; evaluation is limited to NVS photometric metrics and open-vocabulary mIoU/mAcc on indoor ScanNet data only. Claims of 'accurate geometry' and generalization to Internet video (the motivation for the dataset) are untested; all evaluation is on the indoor scan domain that also comprises the training set.

Baseline fairness concerns: 2-view feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R) are adapted to multi-view via a DUSt3R-style post-processing scheme whose details are not given, and per-scene baselines in Table 2 are compared only on mIoU/mAcc, not on NVS quality; LSeg is compared using ground-truth novel views. Several comparisons thus favor the proposed method without clear evidence the baselines were tuned equivalently.

Key implementation details are missing (semantic feature dimension D, SH degree k, voxel sizes epsilon_geo/epsilon_sem, coverage threshold tau, training compute/duration, GPU memory), the project page is empty, and no code or dataset release is stated, undermining reproducibility. The 3D editing capability is shown only as a figure with no method or quantitative evaluation.

Ablations are incomplete and conducted only on ScanNet++: no ablation of the hierarchical sparsification design choices (voxel sizes, isotropic vs. anisotropic fusion, moment matching), no comparison of the instance contrastive loss against a pixel-wise contrastive baseline to substantiate the claimed O(N_p K) efficiency benefit, and no analysis of the novel-view selection threshold tau.

Presentation quality is below ECCV standards: several grammatical errors ('are struggle to handle', 'preatrained'), an empty 'Project page:' link, and somewhat sparse treatment of the sparsification section relative to its centrality to the contribution. Claimed multi-task capability ('various related tasks') exceeds what is actually evaluated (NVS + open-vocabulary segmentation).

strengths: Strong practical contribution: FLEG is a unified feed-forward model that reconstructs language-embedded Gaussians from uncalibrated, unposed inputs spanning sparse (2) to dense (32+) views, addressing a real limitation of existing feed-forward language-field methods that are tied to fixed two-view inputs or require camera parameters.

The 3D-annotation-free training framework is a thoughtful design: novel-view selection via coverage masks enables photometric supervision on held-out views without GT poses, which is a sensible way to get cross-view consistency supervision from 2D video data.

InstanceMV-14K (15M+ images, ~14K scenes with instance masks from scans and Internet video) is a valuable resource enabled by the annotation-free framework, and the instance-guided contrastive loss is well motivated with a clear complexity analysis (O(NpK) vs O(Np^2)).

The geometry–semantic hierarchical sparsification strategy is a non-trivial and well-reasoned contribution: decoupling semantic from geometric Gaussian density via voxelization with smaller semantic voxels, moment-matched isotropic fusion, and confidence-weighted softmax aggregation is technically sound and ablations show it reduces semantic Gaussian count (6.4M → 2.6M) with no quality loss.

Empirical results are convincing: consistent gains over feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R, LSeg) across all view counts on both PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS and open-vocabulary mIoU/mAcc, plus large efficiency advantage over per-scene optimization (seconds vs ~10–20 minutes) while also achieving higher query accuracy (Tab. 2).

Stable performance as view count increases (unlike baselines that degrade sharply) directly supports the 'any views' claim; the paper also clearly differentiates itself from closely related concurrent work (EA3D, IGGT).
weaknesses: Heavy architectural and training dependence on VGGT raises a circularity concern: the model is initialized from VGGT, distills VGGT pseudo-labels (point maps, poses) for geometry, and uses VGGT-predicted point maps for coverage masks, 3D feature aggregation, and target-view selection. The paper does not analyze how much of the geometric quality is inherited versus learned, nor behavior when VGGT's pseudo-labels are wrong (e.g., textureless or reflective regions).

Evaluation scope is narrow: only ScanNet and ScanNet++ indoor scenes. Given the claim of arbitrary unposed Internet-style inputs, results on outdoor or in-the-wild data (e.g., RE10K, one held out for training, or other benchmarks) and geometry metrics (depth/pose accuracy) would substantially strengthen the case; qualitative 3D editing (Fig. 1) has no quantitative evaluation at all.

Baseline comparisons have fairness caveats: several baselines are arXiv preprints run under a DUSt3R-style post-processing they were not designed for, and per-scene optimized baselines (LangSplat, LangScene-X) use dense GT-pose inputs while FLEG's evaluation protocol details (test scenes, CLIP threshold handling for mIoU following LangSplat) are only briefly described. No recent any-view feed-forward method without semantics (e.g., AnySplat) is compared on reconstruction to contextualize NVS quality.

Ablations are incomplete: only the distill loss and semantic components are ablated; the coverage threshold τ, voxel sizes εgeo/εsem, number of context views Nc, dataset composition (scan vs. Internet video), and the isotropic approximation in Eq. (12) are not studied. The 'confidence' predicted by the Gaussian head, central to Eq. (8), is never formally defined in the attribute list of Sec. 3.2.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: LSeg's PSNR/SSIM columns are reported as '-' while it is listed as an NVS-incapable baseline, the ablation table header 'Emed. Num' is a typo, the project page link is empty (reproducibility of the 1B-parameter model and dataset release is uncertain), InstanceMV-14K lacks details on data licensing/ethics for Internet-sourced video, and there is no limitations or societal-impact discussion.

The final hybrid representation (geometry Gaussians plus a separate sparser set of semantic Gaussians) leaves some mechanics under-specified: how the two sets are jointly rasterized during feature-map rendering for the Lfeat loss and at inference, and whether semantic–geometric misalignment at object boundaries is observed, is not explained.

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical gap: prior feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian methods are restricted to two input views or require camera parameters, while FLEG supports 2–32 uncalibrated, unposed views in a single model; this is a meaningful advance for realistic deployment.

The dual-branch distillation framework (VGGT-based geometric distillation + CLIP/SAM2-based semantic distillation) enables training without any 3D ground truth or semantic labels, which is an important enabler for scalable training; the claim of enabling training on arbitrary video/image collections is well supported by the design.

The novel-view-based distillation strategy is a sensible and apparently effective contribution: it provides novel-view supervision without ground-truth poses, and the ablations (Tab. 3, line 5) plus the depth-estimation analysis (Tab. 5) show it mitigates input-view overfitting that affects AnySplat.

The sparsity insight—that language/semantic information is much sparser than geometric information, so per-Gaussian embeddings are unnecessary—is a valuable observation. The DGLE module achieving comparable semantic fidelity with <5% of embeddings and 1/20 storage is practically significant, and the supplementary sparsity sweep (Fig. 5) systematically validates the hypothesis rather than just asserting it.

Experiments are extensive and well-designed: multiple view counts (2/4/8/16/32), two main datasets plus an unseen-dataset (Replica) generalization study, extra comparisons of camera pose and depth estimation, thorough ablations of every major component, and honest reporting of where the method does not beat VGGT (2-view pose, input-view depth) or where baselines beat it (voxel variant mIoU).
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with limitations candidly discussed (dependence on VGGT for geometry, indoor-only training data, memory limits for very large view counts).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the architecture is essentially VGGT plus a DPT Gaussian head following AnySplat (including the voxelization module from AnySplat), and the semantic side combines well-established components (CLIP distillation, SAM2 masks, instance-level contrastive learning). The main genuinely new elements are the novel-view-based distillation and the DGLE module; the paper's impact rests on system integration rather than fundamentally new techniques.

There are inconsistencies and quality issues in the results presentation that undermine confidence: Table 2 contains an obvious typo ('0.79.74') and a suspicious jump on ScanNet (mIoU 60.97, mAcc 91.67 at 32 views vs. ~47–48 mIoU and ~73 mAcc at 2–16 views in Table 1) that is only partially explained by the different (subset) evaluation protocol for Table 2; this protocol difference should be stated in the main text, and the gap warrants explanation or verification.

The headline claim that the compact representation achieves 'comparable or even superior' semantic fidelity is slightly overstated: in the ablation, the voxelized per-Gaussian variant actually achieves higher mIoU (47.83 vs. 46.87) and mAcc (73.14 vs. 72.96); 'comparable' is defensible, 'superior' is not.

Training and evaluation are confined to indoor ScanNet/ScanNet++ (with generalization tested only on Replica, another indoor dataset); cross-dataset generalization claims are therefore limited in scope, and the authors acknowledge this—outdoor or in-the-wild evidence would strengthen the contribution.

The baseline comparison protocol for LSM and Uni3R (using their official two-view models with the two nearest views to the target) is reasonable given architectural constraints but introduces a view-selection advantage that, while following prior work [44], is not fully controlled; a discussion of how sensitive this protocol is would help.

Several minor editorial problems: the project page link in the abstract is empty, 'attributions' is used instead of 'attributes' repeatedly, and there are grammatical errors (e.g., 'Linst belongs to semantic branch'); Eq. (6) notation (positives summed in the numerator) should be checked for the intended multi-positive InfoNCE form.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian methods are limited to two input views or require camera parameters; FLEG addresses flexible-view, pose-free input, which is a practical and relevant gap.

The dual-branch distillation framework is technically sound: novel-view-based distillation using VGGT-predicted coverage masks to select reliable target views is a sensible, pose-free way to obtain novel-view supervision without GT poses, and the coverage-threshold selection (Eqs. 1-3) is well specified.

The instance-guided contrastive loss (Eq. 6) is a useful contribution: it improves instance discriminability over naive CLIP alignment while reducing contrastive complexity from O(N_p^2) to O(N_pK), which matters for feed-forward training.

The semantic-sparsity observation and DGLE module (moment-matched isotropic semantic Gaussians, <5% embeddings, 1/20 storage) is an interesting and well-supported insight; the ablation (Tab. 3 lines 1-3) and the v_sem sweep (Fig. 5, appendix C) directly validate the sparsity hypothesis.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: comparisons across 2-32 input views on ScanNet++, ScanNet, and unseen Replica, plus ablations, camera pose (Tab. 4) and depth (Tab. 5) evaluations, and qualitative figures; results consistently and often substantially outperform feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R, AnySplat) and per-scene methods in segmentation metrics.

The framework requires no 3D ground truth or semantic labels, enabling scalable training; baselines are open-sourced and evaluated under the same training data, supporting fair comparison and reproducibility.
Limitations are honestly discussed (appendix I): dependence on VGGT's geometry ceiling, indoor-only generalization, and memory limits for very large view counts.
weaknesses: Geometric quality is capped by VGGT distillation: at input views, depth (Tab. 5) and at 2-view settings pose accuracy (Tab. 4) are slightly below VGGT; the paper does not demonstrate any path to surpassing the teacher, so the geometry contribution is incremental over AnySplat-style distillation.

The claimed multi-task capabilities include 3D editing ('turn the floor yellow'), but no editing experiment or quantitative evaluation appears anywhere in the paper; this claim is only illustrated in Fig. 1 and should be removed or supported.

Novelty is moderate: the paper is largely a careful combination of existing components (VGGT architecture/heads, AnySplat voxelization, CLIP+SAM distillation, LangSplat-style evaluation); the main original elements are the coverage-based novel-view target selection, instance-anchored contrastive loss, and DGLE.

Protocol caveats for main comparisons: LSM and Uni3R are two-view models evaluated by feeding the two nearest views to the target, which is a somewhat favorable setup for these baselines but also means multi-view baselines are absent; FLEG is the only true multi-view feed-forward semantic method in Tab. 1, weakening the strength of 'outperforms' claims at 8/16 views.

Table 2 has inconsistencies that undermine polish: a malformed value ('0.79.74' for LangSplat SSIM on ScanNet), and Tab. 2's ScanNet++ FLEG numbers (mIoU 46.61) are identical to the 2-view row of Tab. 1, raising questions about averaging or reporting errors; evaluation on a scene subset for Tab. 2 (appendix B) further limits direct comparability.

Some losses and design details are under-specified: L_distill is only described textually in Sec. 4.1/appendix A rather than formalized, the light-weight MLP after feature rendering is not detailed, and DGLE hyperparameters (v_sem, v_geo, embedding dimension D) are only partially covered in the appendix.

Evaluation is limited to indoor scenes and, for training-scale claims ('potential for large-scale training'), no experiment with more diverse or larger-scale data is provided, so the scalability benefit remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

Only semantic sparsity is ablated for DGLE's design choices; alternatives such as learned codebooks or vector quantization for compact semantics (a natural competing approach for storage reduction) are not compared, and DF-3DGS [6], which the paper itself cites as exploring feature sparsity, is not compared against.

strengths: Clear and practical problem formulation: the paper removes two key restrictions of prior feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian methods (fixed two-view inputs and required camera parameters), which is a meaningful step toward real-world applicability (robotics, AR/VR).

The novel-view-based distillation strategy is a sensible and technically sound contribution: it enables novel-view supervision for pose-free feed-forward training without GT cameras, and the ablations (Tab. 3, lines 1/5/6) plus the overfitting analysis vs. AnySplat in the supplementary (Tab. 5) support its effectiveness.

The Decoupled Gaussian Language Embedding (DGLE) and compact semantic representation are a valuable design insight: semantic signals are much sparser than geometry, so per-Gaussian embeddings are unnecessary. The supplementary sparsity analysis (Fig. 5) systematically characterizes the trade-off between v_sem, mIoU, and storage, strengthening the claim.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: comparisons across 2–32 input views on ScanNet++/ScanNet, against feed-forward methods, per-scene optimized methods, and 2D distillation sources; ablations of all major components; camera pose (Tab. 4) and depth (Tab. 5) comparisons; and cross-dataset generalization on Replica (Tab. 6) with reasonable discussion of the training-data asymmetry vs. AnySplat.

The paper is generally well written and organized, with a transparent evaluation protocol (alignment strategy adopted from AnySplat for pose-free evaluation, faithful two-view configurations for fixed-view baselines), and a candid limitations section (indoor-only generalization, VGGT-bounded geometry, memory scaling with input views).
Good attribution: contributions of AnySplat, VGGT, IGGT, DF-3DGS, and prior semantic-sparsity work are appropriately cited and differentiated.
weaknesses: The 'comparable semantic fidelity with <5% of embeddings' claim is not fully supported by the ablation: Tab. 3 shows the voxelized dense variant (line 2) actually achieves higher mIoU (47.83 vs. 46.87) and mAcc (73.14 vs. 72.96) than the compact version. The trade-off is favorable given 20x storage savings, but 'comparable or even superior' overstates the evidence; the claim should be stated more precisely.

The contribution is incremental in places: the architecture is essentially VGGT/AnySplat with an added Gaussian and semantic head, and the semantic-sparsity observation has been partially explored before (DF-3DGS [6] for per-scene 3DGS). The novelty rests mainly on the distillation framework and the feed-forward decoupled embedding, which is sufficient but not groundbreaking.

Training is limited to ScanNet and ScanNet++ (indoor scenes), same as the closest baselines. While the Replica experiment is appreciated, the claimed potential for 'large-scale training on arbitrary video sequences' is asserted but never demonstrated; at least a small-scale experiment on external video data would substantiate this headline claim.

Fairness concerns in baseline comparison remain partially unaddressed: LSM and Uni3R are evaluated with two nearest views to the target rather than their native multi-view setting, and per-scene methods in Tab. 2 are evaluated only on a scene subset. These choices are justified and consistent with prior work, but they make some comparisons less decisive than they appear.

Some technical details are under-specified: the D-dimension of language embeddings and the mapping from C-dim CLIP features to D-dim Gaussian embeddings via the MLP are not clearly defined; the selection threshold tau and voxel size v_geo are not given in the main text; L_distill is only loosely described as 'MSE/Huber between predictions and pseudo-labels' with details split across the appendix.

Minor presentation issues: a typo in Tab. 2 (mAcc '0.79.74' for LangSplat), undefined notation ({M} vs {M_i} in Eq. 1), and Eq. 4 omits an explicit L1/L2 norm symbol in the photometric term. These do not affect the scientific case but should be corrected.

The evaluation of semantics relies on open-vocabulary segmentation of a limited set of object categories per scene; there is no evaluation of fine-grained open-vocabulary retrieval or part-level queries, which would better test the language-alignment quality of the distilled CLIP features.
